what_happened: An operator reverted landing commit 02837e0 (from 2026-10-19) by hand. The first revert also deleted the records the squash had added. The repo's full history check treats records as append-only, so it refused the revert. That cost one extra CI round. The operator then had to redo the revert. No job was rejected.
cause: Athena has `land` for bringing work in but no matching way to undo a landing. A revert is a raw git operation that treats everything a landing touched alike. A landing mixes governed content, which can be reverted, with append-only records, which must stay. Only the history check, which runs late in CI, knows that difference. Nothing at revert time separates the two kinds of file or warns the operator, so the mistake shows up only after a pushed round.
prevention: Add an `athena revert <landing>` command. It would revert only the governed content of that landing and leave all append-only records untouched. It would also write a record of the revert. It would run the history check locally before it pushes anything. Plain hand reverts of a landing would be flagged or refused, so the append-only rule is handled by code and not by operator memory.
proposed_request: Add an `athena revert` command that undoes a landed job. Given a landing commit or job id, it must restore the governed content that landing changed to its prior state. It must not delete or edit any append-only record the landing added, and it must add a new record saying the landing was reverted and why. Before it finishes, it must run the full history check locally and report the result. If the check would fail, it must stop and change nothing. Show it works by reverting a test landing that added both governed content and records: the content goes back, the records stay, and the history check passes. Also show that a plain git revert of that same landing is detected and reported as breaking the append-only rule.
